subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Green, Grey, and Blue Hydrogen
description: A short lesson to help you apply Green, Grey, and Blue Hydrogen.

hook.text: Not all hydrogen is created equal—the color label tells you how clean the production process really is.

buildup.text: Grey hydrogen comes from splitting natural gas, releasing carbon dioxide—this is 95 percent of today's supply.

discovery.text: Blue hydrogen captures that CO2 before it escapes, but capture technology is expensive and imperfect.

twist.text: Green hydrogen uses renewable electricity to split water, producing zero emissions—but it costs three times more.

climax.text: For hydrogen cars to truly be clean, the world needs massive green hydrogen production that doesn't yet exist.

punchline.text: Hydrogen is only as clean as the energy used to make it.

quiz.question: What makes green hydrogen different from grey hydrogen?
options: It's produced using renewable energy with zero emissions

details.summary: Hydrogen is classified by color based on how it is produced. Green hydrogen uses renewable electricity, blue captures CO2 from natural gas, and grey releases CO2 into the atmosphere.
details.whyItMatters: Over 95 percent of hydrogen today is grey, meaning it generates significant emissions. Scaling green hydrogen is essential if fuel-cell cars are to become a truly clean alternative.
takeaways: Green hydrogen is made by electrolysis using renewable power
Blue hydrogen captures carbon from natural gas reforming
Grey hydrogen is cheapest but creates substantial CO2

faq.question: Why does the color of hydrogen matter for cars?
faq.answer: A fuel-cell car is only as clean as its fuel. If the hydrogen was produced from natural gas without carbon capture, the car's well-to-wheel emissions can rival those of a conventional vehicle.

faq.question: Is green hydrogen affordable enough for mass adoption?
faq.answer: Not yet. Green hydrogen costs roughly two to three times more than grey hydrogen, though falling renewable energy prices and electrolyzer scaling are steadily closing the gap.
